effect: Kills by liver failure. Onset 6-24 hr after eating, feels fine in between the first GI wave and the organ failure that follows.
key_features: Cap greenish-yellow to olive-brown (sometimes whitish), smooth, sticky when wet; white gills, free from the stem; white spore print; a skirt-like ring on the upper stem; a sac-like volva at the base, often partly buried -- this is why the base must be dug out, not cut.
habitat_substrate: Ectomycorrhizal with oaks and other hardwoods (introduced to the West Coast with ornamental/orchard trees); ground, never wood.
season_west_coast: Fall, into early winter in mild years.
range_notes: Established and actively spreading in coastal California and documented in the Portland, OR metro area and reappearing in Oregon in multiple seasons. Not a someday risk for this region -- it is here now.
confused_with: Young button stage can resemble an unopened puffball from outside (cut it in half top to bottom); mature caps have been mistaken for edible Volvariella (paddy straw) and for some Agaricus (meadow/horse mushroom) by inexperienced foragers who did not check for a volva.
cannot_determine_from_photo: Whether the base has a volva if it was picked/cut instead of dug; spore print color if none was taken.
distinguishing_test: Dig up the whole base. White gills + ring + volva + white spore print on a mushroom growing from soil near hardwoods = treat as death cap until an expert says otherwise.

citations.title: MykoWeb: Toxic Fungi of Western North America
Mushrooms Up! (Beaty Museum, UBC) - Amanita phalloides
Deadly mushroom reappears in Oregon - Lewiston Tribune

effect: Kills by liver failure, same amatoxin mechanism and timeline as death cap.
key_features: All-white to cream, sometimes with a pale tan/pinkish center on the cap; white gills, free; white spore print; ring on the stem (can be fragile/fall off); sac-like volva at the base.
habitat_substrate: Ground, mycorrhizal with oaks, also reported with other trees; ground only, never wood.
season_west_coast: Late winter through spring, earlier than most of the summer/fall species -- the spring all-white mushroom to take most seriously.
range_notes: Native West Coast species, California through Oregon and Washington.
confused_with: All-white edible Agaricus species (meadow/horse mushroom) by foragers who do not check gill color (Agaricus gills are pink to chocolate-brown at maturity, never white) or who miss the volva; also confused with puffball buttons before it opens.
cannot_determine_from_photo: Gill color if immature/unopened; volva presence if base was cut, not dug.
distinguishing_test: Any all-white mushroom on the ground in spring with white (not pink or brown) gills and any hint of a basal sac gets treated as this until ruled out. Cut immature buttons in half top to bottom to check they are uniform puffball flesh inside, not a developing cap/gills.

citations.title: MykoWeb: Toxic Fungi of Western North America

effect: Kills by liver failure, same amatoxin class as the Amanitas above.
key_features: Small brown mushroom (a genuine LBM), cap tan to rusty-brown, sticky when wet; rusty-brown spore print (this alone rules out Psilocybe, whose spore print is dark purple-brown to blackish -- always ask for a spore print if the candidate differential includes both); thin ring on the stem that can disappear with age or handling.
habitat_substrate: Wood -- dead conifer logs, stumps, buried wood and wood chips/mulch. Grows in clusters or scattered, often right alongside or mixed in with the things it's confused for.
season_west_coast: Late summer through fall, into winter in mild areas.
range_notes: Widespread across the West Coast conifer belt.
confused_with: The highest-stakes confusion in this entire database. (1) Psilocybe species growing on the same wood/mulch substrates -- spore print color is the fast, reliable separator (rusty brown vs dark purple-black); relevant directly in Oregon given licensed psilocybin services and continued interest in wild finds. (2) Honey mushroom (Armillaria) -- both grow in clusters on wood; Armillaria has a much more substantial ring, white spore print, and typically a more robust stature, but the overlap is real enough that any wood-growing cluster ID should get a spore print before anything else.
cannot_determine_from_photo: Spore print color -- this is close to mandatory to ask for whenever Galerina is in the differential.
distinguishing_test: Spore print. Rusty-brown = treat as Galerina-possible and stop. Dark purple-brown/black = not Galerina, still confirm the rest of the ID. White = likely Armillaria territory but still confirm ring/stature.

citations.title: MykoWeb: Toxic Fungi of Western North America

scientific_name: Lepiota subincarnata and related small Lepiotas
effect: Kills by liver failure, amatoxin class.
key_features: Small parasol-shaped LBM, cap often with a pinkish or reddish-brown tint and fine scales, white to cream gills, white spore print. Easy to dismiss as too small/cute to be dangerous -- resist that.
habitat_substrate: Ground, often in grass, mulched beds, and disturbed soil near buildings -- notably a suburban/garden-adjacent risk, not only deep-woods.
range_notes: Less commonly reported than the Amanitas above but genuinely present; sourcing on West Coast-specific incidence is thinner than for Amanita phalloides, treat the caution as categorical rather than frequency-based.
confused_with: Edible small Lepiota-relatives and immature parasol mushrooms by foragers going on size/shape alone without spore-printing.
cannot_determine_from_photo: Precise species within small Lepiota-group without spore print and often microscopy.
distinguishing_test: No reliable field test for a novice. Categorical rule: do not eat small LBM-type Lepiotas on visual ID alone, period -- this genus needs an expert with a microscope.

citations.title: MykoWeb: Toxic Fungi of Western North America
Amatoxin-Containing Mushroom Poisonings: Species, Toxidromes, Treatments, and Outcomes - Diaz, Wilderness & Environmental Medicine 2018

effect: Kills by liver failure, amatoxin class.
key_features: Small, slender, tawny-brown conical cap on a thin fibrous stem with a fragile ring; rusty-brown spore print.
habitat_substrate: Ground -- classically lawns, mossy areas, and grassy disturbed ground, not deep forest.
season_west_coast: Fall, can appear after lawn watering/rain in mixed seasons.
range_notes: PNW lawns and mossy ground specifically called out in regional sources.
confused_with: Mistaken for small Psilocybe or Panaeolus species growing in similar grassy habitat by people specifically looking for those.
cannot_determine_from_photo: Spore print color, stem/ring detail at the needed resolution.
distinguishing_test: No reliable novice field test. Any small tawny conical lawn mushroom being considered for consumption needs a spore print at minimum and expert confirmation. Sourcing on this entry is thinner (mostly enthusiast/field reference sites rather than peer-reviewed) -- taxonomy and toxin claim are well-established in the mycological community but worth a second look if it matters for a real decision.

citations.title: Amatoxin-Containing Mushroom Poisonings: Species, Toxidromes, Treatments, and Outcomes - Diaz, Wilderness & Environmental Medicine 2018

effect: Kills by kidney failure. Onset is the most dangerous kind: 36 hours to 3 weeks, average around 8 days. Someone can eat this, feel completely fine for a week, and then be in irreversible kidney failure.
key_features: Cap tawny-orange to reddish-brown, conical to bell-shaped; rusty-brown spore print; a cobweb-like partial veil (the cortina the genus is named for) instead of a true ring -- often only visible on young specimens.
habitat_substrate: Ground, conifer forest, mycorrhizal.
range_notes: The genus Cortinarius is large and well-represented in West Coast conifer forests. Confirmed North American orellanine poisoning cases are rare in the literature -- a 2020 Quebec case (only the second confirmed orellanine poisoning documented in North America at the time) caused acute kidney failure requiring hospitalization after an 18-day delayed onset, with incomplete kidney recovery at last follow-up. Rarity of documented cases reflects how few North American poisonings get correctly traced back to a Cortinarius meal given the multi-week delay, not evidence the risk is lower here than in Europe, where the case literature is much larger.
confused_with: Novices sometimes lump orange mushroom in the woods together with chanterelles or edible boletes without checking gill structure (this genus has true attached gills, unlike a chanterelle's false ridges) or spore print color.
cannot_determine_from_photo: Spore print, and functionally nothing else matters once Cortinarius is even plausible.
distinguishing_test: None suitable for field use by a non-expert. Any Cortinarius-type mushroom (cobwebby veil remnant, rusty spore print, orange/brown/purple coloring, ground-growing near conifers) is a hard no for consumption, always.

citations.title: A Rare Cortinarius rubellus Poisoning in North America - NAMA

effect: Same toxin, same 36-hour-to-3-week onset, same kidney failure outcome, same no-field-test conclusion as C. rubellus. Listed separately because it is the other species most consistently named alongside C. rubellus in the orellanine literature; European records are denser than North American ones for this species specifically.
key_features: See Deadly Webcap -- same genus-level cautions apply.
habitat_substrate: Ground, conifer forest, mycorrhizal.
range_notes: European records denser than North American for this species specifically.
distinguishing_test: Same as Deadly Webcap -- no field test, hard no on any Cortinarius-type find.

scientific_name: Gyromitra esculenta and western relatives (G. montana, G. ambigua, G. infula)
effect: Gyromitrin converts in the body to monomethylhydrazine (MMH) -- chemically related to rocket fuel -- causing liver, kidney, and blood-cell damage in serious cases; also implicated as carcinogenic. Onset 2-24 hr. Toxin is partly volatile, which is exactly why some people parboil and eat these safely is not a safety protocol, it's variable-dose Russian roulette.
key_features: Cap wrinkled/brain-like or saddle-shaped (not the honeycomb-pitted cap of a true morel), reddish-brown to dark brown; stem often chambered or cottony inside rather than fully hollow.
habitat_substrate: Ground, conifer forest, often at similar elevations and in similar burned/disturbed habitat to true spring morels -- the single most dangerous timing/habitat overlap in this database for anyone who forages morels in the Cascades or northern Rockies.
season_west_coast: Spring, overlapping true morel season, often slightly earlier or at similar elevation bands.
range_notes: G. montana specifically is a western mountain species fruiting with spring snowmelt at elevation, directly inside classic spring king bolete and natural morel territory.
confused_with: True morels (Morchella species). This is the pairing to check first any time morel comes up as a candidate in spring.
cannot_determine_from_photo: Whether the cap is truly honeycomb-pitted (morel) vs wrinkled/brain-like (Gyromitra) can be ambiguous in a poor-quality or top-down-only photo -- ask for a cross-section photo. This is the single highest-value extra photo for spring finds: a true morel is completely hollow from cap tip to stem base; Gyromitra is chambered or cottony inside.
distinguishing_test: Cut it in half top to bottom. Hollow all the way through = consistent with true morel. Chambered, cottony, or brain-like/lobed cap surface instead of true pits = treat as Gyromitra.

citations.title: Gyromitra esculenta - Mushrooms Up! (Beaty Museum, UBC)

effect: Delayed kidney failure, sometimes needing transplant. Onset 4-11 hr -- faster than orellanine but still delayed enough that people eat a second helping before symptoms start.
key_features: White to cream, cottony/shaggy cap surface, bulbous base with cottony volva remnants (often looks like loose ragged tissue rather than a clean sac), white gills, white spore print. Firm white flesh -- this is exactly why it fools people.
habitat_substrate: Ground, ectomycorrhizal with conifers -- the same forests and often the same season as the mushrooms it's mistaken for.
season_west_coast: Fall, overlapping matsutake and king bolete season.
range_notes: Pacific Northwest specialty risk. Not a generic Amanitas are bad entry -- a specific, repeatedly documented clinical problem among PNW matsutake and king bolete harvesters.
confused_with: Matsutake (Tricholoma murrillianum) and spring/fall king bolete before the pores develop -- both grow in the same conifer duff, both can present as a firm white-ish mushroom pushing up through soil, and harvesters working fast in low light picking by feel/silhouette are the documented at-risk group. Multiple published case series exist on exactly this confusion.
cannot_determine_from_photo: Whether the base was fully excavated; bolete candidates specifically need the underside checked for pores (spongy, not gills) vs this species' true gills.
distinguishing_test: Dig the entire base out, do not cut at soil level. True gills (not pores/sponge) plus a cottony/shaggy ragged basal volva rules matsutake and king bolete out entirely and should stop the harvest right there.

citations.title: Acute renal failure associated with suspected Amanita smithiana ingestions - case series, PubMed
Amanita smithiana ingestion: delayed renal failure - Journal of Medical Toxicology

effect: Severe gastrointestinal distress -- nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and sensory disturbances, roughly 5-10 hr after eating in most reports (large doses can come on faster). The mushroom's own intensely bitter taste is a built-in warning most people won't ignore once they chew a piece, but bitterness can't be confirmed from a photo alone.
key_features: Cap 1-6 cm, light yellow to yellow-brown, darkening with age; gills yellow with a green cast when young, dark grey-purple at maturity; dark purple-black spore print; grows in dense clusters on dead wood.
habitat_substrate: Wood -- stumps, logs, buried roots, both conifer and hardwood; saprotrophic, and very often the exact same substrate as honey mushroom.
season_west_coast: Active across the fall mushroom season, into winter in mild spells -- overlapping honey mushroom's window.
range_notes: Widespread and common across the West Coast wherever there is dead wood to grow on.
confused_with: Honey mushroom (Armillaria spp, Tier C below) by foragers going on "clustered mushroom on wood" alone. Gill color at maturity (yellow-green to purple-grey here vs white on Armillaria) and spore print (dark purple-black here vs white) separate them cleanly. Taste is also a fast, safe field check for this specific pairing -- but never substitute taste for a spore print when Deadly Galerina (Tier A) is also plausible on the same wood.
cannot_determine_from_photo: Gill color at full maturity, spore print color, bitterness.
distinguishing_test: Spore print first. Dark purple-black = consistent with sulfur tuft, not Galerina (rusty-brown) or Armillaria (white). Once Galerina is ruled out by spore print, a cautious taste test (tiny piece, chew briefly, spit out, rinse) can confirm: intensely, unmistakably bitter = sulfur tuft; mild = Armillaria territory, keep confirming.

citations.title: Hypholoma fasciculare - Mushrooms Up! (Beaty Museum, UBC)

effect: Vomiting, nausea, diarrhea, and colicky cramps, typically 30 min - 3 hr after eating; self-limited, resolving once it passes through the system. The species name is literal.
key_features: Cap 4-10 cm, red to pink (sometimes fading to cream with yellow blotching), convex becoming flat with a central depression, grooved margin, peelable cuticle; gills white, crowded, adnate; stem white, brittle, stuffed rather than hollow. Flesh overall is very brittle -- it snaps rather than bends. Tastes sharply peppery-hot when chewed.
habitat_substrate: Ground, ectomycorrhizal, conifer forest -- mossy ground generally, not the bog-only habitat older field guides sometimes suggest.
range_notes: What gets called "Russula emetica" on the West Coast is usually the regional look-alike R. silvicola rather than the more circumboreal, bog-associated R. emetica sensu stricto -- treat any hot-tasting red Russula in West Coast conifer woods as this group rather than trying to pin the exact species from a photo.
confused_with: Edible red-capped Russula species, several of which are genuinely choice. Taste is the fast, safe separator here specifically because the genus Russula carries no amatoxin or orellanine risk once you've confirmed it's actually a Russula (gills, not pores or teeth; brittle flesh that snaps) -- a small taste-and-spit is a legitimate field test for this genus in a way it is never appropriate for an Amanita or Cortinarius.
cannot_determine_from_photo: Taste, which is the primary field separator within this genus.
distinguishing_test: Taste a tiny piece of raw flesh, chew a few seconds, spit out, rinse the mouth. Sharp, burning, peppery = Sickener group, do not eat. Mild or nutty = a different Russula, still confirm color and spore print before eating.

citations.title: Russula emetica - Mushrooms Up! (Beaty Museum, UBC)

effect: Gastrointestinal upset if eaten raw or undercooked -- the species name (torminosus, "causing colic") is a direct description. Some traditions pickle and salt this species before eating to neutralize the irritant; that is a food-preparation technique with real failure modes, not a safety guarantee, and this skill does not endorse relying on it for an ID made from a photo.
key_features: Cap 5-15 cm, buff-pink with a distinctly woolly, shaggy, inrolled margin and faint concentric zoning; gills shortly decurrent, crowded, pale pink, exuding white to pale cream latex when cut; stem paler than the cap, becoming hollow with age.
habitat_substrate: Ground, mycorrhizal specifically with birch -- the birch association is a useful habitat check on its own.
range_notes: Well documented in Europe; North American populations including the West Coast are reported but less densely studied -- treat the toxicity caution as solid and the exact regional frequency as less certain.
confused_with: Other pink-to-orange latex-exuding Lactarius species, some of which are considered edible. The woolly, shaggy, inrolled cap margin is the fastest visual separator from smoother-margined Lactarius look-alikes.
cannot_determine_from_photo: Latex color and taste if not reported; birch association if habitat context is missing.
distinguishing_test: Cap margin texture (woolly/shaggy = this species) plus confirmed birch habitat. As with any milk-cap genus member, do not rely on visual ID alone -- latex color, taste, and staining reaction all matter and none are safely guessable from a photo.

citations.title: Lactarius torminosus, Woolly Milkcap - First Nature

common_name: Early False Morel / Wrinkled Thimble Morel
effect: Safety is genuinely disputed, not settled science. Unlike Gyromitra (Tier A above), Verpa bohemica has not been confirmed to contain gyromitrin, and some regions (parts of northern Italy) have a tradition of eating it. North American mycological sources still routinely flag it as suspect, with scattered reports of GI upset and, less consistently, transient loss of coordination after eating it -- most often associated with repeated meals over several days rather than a single serving. Given the real uncertainty here, plus the confusion risk with true morels below, this skill treats it as a caution-flag species rather than a confirmed edible or a confirmed poison -- don't state a verdict either way, say plainly that it's disputed.
key_features: Cap wrinkled/brain-like, thimble-shaped, and attached to the stem ONLY at the very top -- the free-hanging skirt-like margin is the single most distinctive feature and the fastest way to separate it from a true morel. Stem filled with cottony pith, not hollow; pale ocher to buff, often with fine whitish granules or chevrons on the surface.
habitat_substrate: Ground, with a classic association with black cottonwood (Populus trichocarpa) riparian zones -- leaf litter and duff along rivers and streams.
season_west_coast: The earliest of the spring morel-type fruitings, typically 2-4 weeks ahead of true morels at the same site -- useful as a seasonal indicator for morel hunters, not as a reason to assume it's safe to eat.
range_notes: Found across Cascadia, more frequently reported in inland valleys and east-side river systems than immediately coastal areas.
confused_with: True morels (Morchella spp, Tier C below) by anyone keying on general size and color rather than checking the cap's attachment point and doing a cross-section -- this pairing is the entire reason this species is in the database.
cannot_determine_from_photo: Cap-to-stem attachment is sometimes visible in a good photo, but the stem interior (cottony vs. hollow) needs a cross-section to confirm.
distinguishing_test: Check where the cap attaches to the stem. Only at the very top, with the margin hanging free = Verpa bohemica. Attached most of the way down, fused to the stem = true morel. A cross-section confirms it: cottony pith-filled stem = Verpa; one continuous hollow chamber from cap tip to stem base = true morel.

citations.title: Toxicity of PNW Morels and False Morels - Salish Mushrooms
Verpa bohemica: Wrinkled Thimble Morel - Salish Mushrooms
Warning on False or True Morels and Button Mushrooms with Potential Toxicity Linked to Hydrazinic Toxins: An Update - MDPI Toxins

effect: Severe gastroenteritis -- vomiting, cramping, watery diarrhea, starting 1-3 hr after eating. The single most common cause of mushroom poisoning calls in North America, by volume, ahead of every Tier A species combined -- not because it's more dangerous, but because it's common, grows in lawns and disturbed ground right where people encounter it, and looks enough like edible parasol mushrooms to fool people who go on shape alone.
key_features: Large white parasol-shaped mushroom, scaly cap, but the spore print is green to grayish-green -- this is the one reliable field test and it is easy to run.
habitat_substrate: Ground, classically suburban lawns, golf courses, parks -- fairy rings are common.
season_west_coast: Summer through fall, especially after irrigation or rain following heat.
confused_with: Shaggy parasol and true parasol mushrooms (Macrolepiota), which are white-spored and edible for most people.
distinguishing_test: Spore print. White = parasol group, still confirm further. Green/gray-green = Chlorophyllum molybdites, do not eat.

citations.title: UF/IFAS Extension PP324: The Green-Spore Poison Parasol Mushroom

effect: CNS effects -- confusion, visual distortion, agitation, can progress to sedation or coma-like sleep lasting hours; onset 30 min - 2 hr. Rarely fatal in healthy adults but genuinely dangerous, especially in children, the elderly, or in combination with alcohol/other substances. Atropine (the muscarine antidote) is contraindicated here -- different toxin despite the name similarity.
key_features: Iconic red-with-white-spots cap (can fade to orange/yellow). White gills, a ring, and a volva that often breaks into a series of shaggy rings at the base rather than a clean sac.
habitat_substrate: Ground, mycorrhizal with conifers and some hardwoods.
season_west_coast: Fall, iconic and extremely commonly photographed -- expect this to come up often purely because it's the mushroom everyone recognizes and photographs, not necessarily because someone intends to eat it.

citations.title: Amanita Mushrooms of the PNW - Salish Mushrooms

effect: Same isoxazole syndrome as Fly Agaric, but A. pantherina generally causes more severe poisoning than A. muscaria and should be treated with equal or greater caution.
key_features: Brown cap with white warts, more subdued coloring than Fly Agaric. White gills, a ring, and a volva that often breaks into shaggy rings rather than a clean sac.
habitat_substrate: Ground, mycorrhizal with conifers and some hardwoods.

citations.title: Amanita Mushrooms of the PNW - Salish Mushrooms

effect: Severe GI distress -- nausea (~90% of cases), vomiting (~73%), cramping, headache; onset 1-3 hr; recovery typically within 12 hr, rarely fatal.
key_features: The chanterelle look-alike that matters most on the West Coast. Bright orange, funnel-shaped, grows in dense clustered clumps. True gills that are thin, blade-like, and closely spaced, running down the stem -- versus a chanterelle's false gills, which are blunt, forked, vein-like ridges, not true blades. Fresh specimens can be bioluminescent (faintly glow in total darkness) -- a fun field test if conditions allow, not a substitute for the gill check.
habitat_substrate: Grows on wood -- buried roots, stumps, dead wood, often looking like it's coming out of the ground when it's actually attached to buried wood/roots. Chanterelles grow from the ground, mycorrhizal with living trees, never from wood. Clustered growth (many fruiting bodies from one base) is typical here and unusual for chanterelles.
season_west_coast: Fall, same general window as chanterelle season.
range_notes: O. olivascens is the West Coast species (California through Oregon); the similarly-named O. olearius is more an eastern US/European species -- don't cite olearius-specific range claims for a West Coast find.
confused_with: Chanterelle (Cantharellus spp) -- see lookalike pairs table.
cannot_determine_from_photo: Whether the base is attached to buried wood/roots vs free in soil.
distinguishing_test: Dig around the base. Attached to wood/roots = Jack O'Lantern territory. Free in soil, no wood connection = consistent with chanterelle, keep checking the gill structure to be sure.

citations.title: Jack O'Lantern Mushrooms: A Poisonous Chanterelle Look-Alike

scientific_name: Inocybe spp, Clitocybe dealbata / C. rivulosa
effect: The SLUDGE pattern -- salivation, lacrimation (tearing), sweating, GI distress, visual problems, irregular pulse; onset fast, 15-30 min. Treatable with atropine under medical care, but this is a genuine ER visit, not a wait-it-out situation.
key_features: Mostly small-to-medium brown (Inocybe, often fibrous-capped and spindle-shaped) or small white (Clitocybe, funnel-shaped, in lawns/grass) mushrooms -- functionally the general unidentified small brown or small white mushroom caution zone.
habitat_substrate: Ground; Clitocybe dealbata/rivulosa specifically in lawns and grassy areas, sometimes in fairy rings.
distinguishing_test: Treat this whole zone as a do-not-eat-without-expert-confirmation area rather than trying to pin an exact species from a casual photo.

effect: Not dangerous on its own -- the danger is entirely about alcohol. Coprine reacts with alcohol consumed anywhere from the same meal up to about 5 days later, causing an Antabuse-like reaction: flushing, rapid heartbeat, tingling, palpitations.
key_features: Grayish, oval-to-bell cap that liquefies into black ink as it ages (the inky cap group); grows in clusters from the ground, often near buried wood/roots or in disturbed soil.
habitat_substrate: Ground, often near buried wood/roots or in disturbed soil.
confused_with: Shaggy mane (Coprinus comatus, Tier C, edible and also an inky cap): shaggy mane has a shaggy, scaly white-to-tan cap; Coprinopsis atramentaria is smoother and gray-brown. Shaggy mane causes its own milder, less well-characterized alcohol-adjacent GI upset in some people, a different and lesser issue than true coprine syndrome.
distinguishing_test: No alcohol within several days of eating any inky-cap-type mushroom, regardless of which one it is, until the exact species is confirmed.

effect: Unlike everything else in this database, dangerous through cumulative repeated exposure, not a single meal. Some people develop an immune reaction after eating it multiple times over months or years, then experience acute hemolytic anemia (the immune system attacking red blood cells) on a later exposure -- sometimes severe enough to be fatal, and easy to misdiagnose as unrelated anemia since the mushroom connection isn't obvious.
key_features: Brown, funnel-shaped cap with a distinctly inrolled (involuted) margin; gills that are decurrent and can be peeled from the cap flesh, often browning/staining where bruised.
habitat_substrate: Ground, mycorrhizal.
range_notes: This species was eaten as a safe when cooked mushroom in parts of Europe for decades before the delayed immune mechanism was understood -- the single best illustration in this database of why I've eaten this before with no problem is not a safety test.

key_features: Large red-burgundy to maroon cap fading paler with age; gills dark purple-grey at maturity; purple-black spore print; a thick, wavy, membranous ring on a white stem.
habitat_substrate: Wood-chip mulch beds, landscaped and gardened areas -- a genuinely urban/garden find as often as a woodland one; saprotrophic.
season_west_coast: Summer through fall, especially in irrigated or mulched beds.
watch_for: No well-established dangerous look-alike once cap color, gill color, and the substantial ring are all confirmed together -- but confirm all three, not just the cap. Check for small holes indicating fly larvae, which spoil a specimen fast (a quality issue, not a safety one). As with any new-to-you species, try a small amount the first time given occasional individual sensitivity.

citations.title: Stropharia rugosoannulata - Midwest American Mycological Information

cap_size: 4-14 cm diameter, starting convex/bell-shaped and flattening with age.
stem_size: 8-18 cm long x 1-2.5 cm thick, roughly equal width, with a large, distinctive radially-grooved (cogwheel-like) ring.
flesh_characteristics: Flesh is white, firm, and unchanging in color when cut or bruised.

key_features: Dark reddish-brown to maroon-brown cap with a rough, velvety texture; stem club-shaped with a swollen base, dark brown with paler streaks; pores pale yellow when young, darkening to dingy olive-yellow with age.
habitat_substrate: Unusual for a bolete: grows from well-decayed, moss-covered wood (hemlock logs and stumps) rather than open ground, though it can look terrestrial when the wood is buried.
season_west_coast: Fall, peaking in October, with the first flush roughly 2-3 weeks after significant fall rains.
range_notes: Common throughout western Washington, Oregon, and coastal BC in mossy, mature hemlock-associated forest, sea level to about 4,000 ft.
watch_for: General bolete caution still applies regardless of species-level confidence: avoid anything with red/orange pores that bruise blue (see the caution under fall king bolete for the toxic Boletus/Suillellus group this rules out). This species does not match that pattern, but confirm pore color and bruising before eating any bolete. Its wood-growing habit is unusual for the genus -- don't treat "grows from soil" as a given bolete identifier here.

citations.title: Admirable Bolete - Kitsap Peninsula Mycological Society
Admirable Bolete - Kitsap Peninsula Mycological Society

cap_size: 7-14 cm diameter, convex expanding to plano-convex, velvety reddish-brown surface.
stem_size: 7-14 cm long x 2-4 cm thick, narrowed toward the top and enlarged at the base.
flesh_characteristics: Flesh is unchanging where cut/exposed; unlike most boletes, the pores/tubes do NOT bruise blue, a key diagnostic feature.

key_features: Tooth fungus -- spines, not gills or pores, on the underside; brown scaly/shingled cap, brown spore print, a strong distinctive mushroomy smell.
habitat_substrate: Ground, ectomycorrhizal with conifers, often at higher elevation.
range_notes: West Coast material is commonly called by this name in regional field guides, though there is some question in the mycological literature about whether North American populations are genuinely the same species as European Sarcodon imbricatus or a distinct, less formally described West Coast lineage -- treat the species-level name here as regionally conventional rather than fully settled.
watch_for: Flavor and edibility both decline with age and size -- pick young specimens. A related species (Sarcodon scabrosus) is more strongly bitter and some people react poorly to it; taste a tiny raw piece and spit it out before committing a whole harvest -- pronounced bitterness is a reason to skip that batch, not something to cook through.

citations.title: Trial field key to the species of Sarcodon in the Pacific Northwest - Pacific Northwest Key Council

cap_size: Sources disagree modestly on the upper bound: PNW Key Council's trial key gives 5-20 cm; MykoWeb (California Fungi) gives 5-25 cm.
stem_size: Roughly 3.5-8 cm long x 2-3.5 cm thick, whitish when young, becoming brownish and velvety-textured toward the base.
flesh_characteristics: Thick, cream-to-buff or whitish-gray-brown flesh, no bruising reaction when cut; taste ranges mild to notably bitter, increasing with age.

key_features: Orange-yellow, funnel shape, blunt false gills (forked ridges, not blades), fruity apricot smell, white-ish flesh
habitat_substrate: Ground, mycorrhizal (Douglas fir, hemlock)
watch_for: Western Jack-O-Lantern -- see lookalike pairs table

citations.title: Cantharellus formosus - Pacific golden chanterelle (Beaty Biodiversity Museum, UBC)

cap_size: 3-10 cm diameter typically, though mature specimens up to ~15 cm are sometimes reported; convex becoming flat or shallowly depressed with wavy, often false-gilled margins.
stem_size: 4-6 cm long x up to 1.5 cm thick at the apex, tapering downward, continuous with the cap with no clear cap/stem demarcation.
flesh_characteristics: Whitish to pale yellowish flesh; cap and stem base often bruise yellowish to brownish -- a mild, non-blackening reaction.

key_features: Small, brown-yellow cap, hollow yellow stem, thin gill-like ridges
habitat_substrate: Ground, mossy conifer forest
watch_for: Generally low-risk group, still confirm ridges not true gills
cap_size: 2-7 cm diameter, convex at first, becoming vase-shaped with an eventual central perforation.
stem_size: 3-9 cm long x 0.3-0.8 cm thick, fairly uniform width, becoming hollow with age; the stem is characteristically yellow ("yellowfoot"), a key field mark.
flesh_characteristics: Thin, insubstantial flesh, brownish to yellowish; no notable bruising or latex reaction reported.

key_features: Reddish-brown cap, white-to-yellow pores (not gills) that don't bruise strongly blue, thick reticulated stem
habitat_substrate: Ground, conifer, mid-high elevation
watch_for: Amanita smithiana if pores misread as gills before opening -- see lookalike pairs table

citations.title: Oregon's Spring Bolete - Cascade Mycological Society

cap_size: 9-18 cm diameter, reddish-brown, a notably large robust bolete ("hamburger-bun" shaped cap), sometimes with a whitish bloom at the margin when young.
stem_size: 5-10 cm long x 2-6 cm thick, stout, often with fine reticulation (net-like pattern) on the upper portion.
flesh_characteristics: White flesh, unchanging when cut; the pore surface does NOT bruise blue, distinguishing it from some other bolete species that stain blue on handling.

key_features: Same pore/reticulation features as spring king
habitat_substrate: Ground, conifer/mixed forest
watch_for: Avoid any bolete with red/orange pores that bruise blue -- flags the Boletus/Suillellus satan's bolete toxic group, not covered in depth here, treat as a stop sign
cap_size: 7-25 cm diameter, brown, greasy-to-tacky, bald cap surface.
stem_size: 7-20 cm long x 3-8 cm thick, swollen/bulbous meaty stem with fine reticulation.
flesh_characteristics: Thick, white flesh, unchanging -- does not stain or bruise on cutting or handling, a key trait separating it from toxic bitter-bolete and blue-staining lookalikes. West Coast "B. edulis group" material is understood to be a species complex, not necessarily identical to true European B. edulis.

key_features: Honeycomb-pitted cap fused to stem, completely hollow top to bottom
habitat_substrate: Ground, variable -- natural stands and post-fire burns
season_west_coast: Spring, elevation-dependent; burn morels 1st spring after fire
watch_for: False morel (Gyromitra, Tier A) -- see lookalike pairs table, most important check in spring

citations.title: Morchellaceae in the Pacific Northwest - Pacific Northwest Key Council
Burn Morel Taxonomy: The 5 Morchella species found in wildfires - Modern Forager

cap_size: Roughly 3-15 cm tall is typical across the West Coast species complex; some yellow-morel taxa (e.g. M. esculentoides) can reach up to ~22 cm tall in ideal conditions -- treat very large specimens as possible but not typical.
stem_size: Roughly 2-12 cm long x 1.5-4 cm thick, hollow, often becoming chambered/layered near the base at maturity.
flesh_characteristics: Cap and stem are completely hollow (single continuous chamber), thin and brittle-waxy flesh, no latex. Most true morels show no bruising, but the West Coast landscaping species M. rufobrunnea is a notable exception -- its young surfaces bruise reddish-orange to salmon.

key_features: Firm white-to-brown scaly cap, distinct spicy-cinnamon smell, substantial ring
habitat_substrate: Ground, conifer (esp. lodgepole/shore pine)
watch_for: Amanita smithiana -- see lookalike pairs table, dig the base every time
cap_size: Sources disagree: MushroomExpert gives 5-10 cm; MykoWeb gives a broader 5-25 cm for mature/robust specimens.
stem_size: MushroomExpert: 4-10 cm long x 1-2.5 cm thick, roughly equal with a slightly tapered base; MykoWeb gives a larger 4-15 cm long x 1-6 cm thick.
flesh_characteristics: Firm white flesh with a strong, distinctive spicy-cinnamon odor; sources differ on staining -- MushroomExpert says flesh doesn't bruise though gills can brown-stain with age, MykoWeb describes the flesh as bruising orange-brown.

key_features: Shelf-shaped, white-gray, gills running down a short/absent stem, white spore print
habitat_substrate: Wood, dead/dying hardwoods
watch_for: Generally low dangerous-lookalike risk on the West Coast; confirm growing on wood, not ground
spore_print_color: White to faintly yellowish or lilac (P. ostreatus); whitish, grayish, or lilac (P. pulmonarius).
cap_size: P. ostreatus: 3-15 cm across; P. pulmonarius: generally smaller, 3-10 cm across.
stem_size: P. ostreatus: stem usually rudimentary and lateral or nearly absent; P. pulmonarius more often has a distinct stem, 1-4 cm long x 0.5-1 cm thick.
flesh_characteristics: Thick, white flesh, unchanging when sliced (no bruising/staining) in both species.

key_features: Bright orange-red crust over a distorted host mushroom shape, dense white interior flesh
habitat_substrate: Ground, parasitizing another mushroom
watch_for: Confirm firm and fully colored -- soft or off-smelling specimens should be skipped regardless of ID

citations.title: Hypomyces lactifluorum - Lobster mushroom (Beaty Biodiversity Museum, UBC)

spore_print_color: Not applicable in the normal sense: this is a parasitic mold (Hypomyces lactifluorum) overgrowing a Russula/Lactifluus host, obliterating its gills, so no conventional spore print can be taken. What's observable instead is an orange-red crust studded with tiny pimple-like perithecia (the parasite's own fruiting structures).
cap_size: Highly variable and irregular, taking the deformed shape of the host mushroom, commonly 5-20+ cm across as a lumpy, brain-like or club/rosette-shaped mass.
stem_size: No normal stem is discernible; the host's stem is typically fused into the same distorted, solid orange mass as the "cap."
flesh_characteristics: Interior flesh is firm and white in fresh specimens, unchanged in color from the original host tissue despite the dramatic external transformation. Aging/rotting specimens soften and can develop a strong fishy odor -- a sign they should not be eaten.

scientific_name: Laetiporus spp (L. gilbertsonii on the West Coast)
key_features: Bright orange-yellow shelf clusters, no gills (pore surface underneath), suede-like texture
habitat_substrate: Wood, living/dead trees
watch_for: West Coast-specific caution: specimens on eucalyptus documented to cause GI upset/allergic-type reactions in some people even when properly cooked -- note the host tree, not just the mushroom
cap_size: Grows as overlapping shelves/brackets rather than a single cap; individual shelves range roughly 7-55 cm broad in aggregate clusters.
stem_size: No true stem: sessile to substipitate, attaching directly to the wood substrate with at most a rudimentary stub.
flesh_characteristics: Flesh 2-3 cm thick, white to yellow when fresh and succulent; no notable bruising/staining, but becomes dry, pale, and crumbly with age.

key_features: Pale orange, spine/tooth surface underneath instead of gills or pores
habitat_substrate: Ground, mycorrhizal
watch_for: Low dangerous-lookalike risk; the tooth surface is distinctive
cap_size: Sources disagree slightly: MushroomExpert gives 6-15 cm wide for H. repandum; MykoWeb gives 2-12 cm; H. umbilicatum is smaller, typically 2-6 cm with a central depression/umbo.
stem_size: Roughly 3-7 cm long x 1-2.5 cm thick, often off-center to central, tapering or equal.
flesh_characteristics: Sources disagree on staining: MushroomExpert describes whitish flesh as unchanging when sliced; MykoWeb describes pale-buff, brittle flesh that bruises buff-orange. The toothed (not gilled) spore-bearing surface underneath the cap is the key diagnostic feature.

key_features: Large, brain/cauliflower-like mass of flat wavy lobes, whitish-tan
habitat_substrate: Ground, base of conifers (often a sign of root rot)
watch_for: Low risk; distinctive form

citations.title: Sparassis radicata - Cauliflower mushroom (Beaty Biodiversity Museum, UBC)

cap_size: Not a discrete cap; the whole convoluted, noodle-like fruitbody measures 10-45 cm across and up to 30 cm high.
stem_size: No true stem in the usual sense: a thick, rooting/radicating stalk-like base up to 30 cm long tapers down into the ground, often attached to a buried conifer root, and is easily left behind during collection.
flesh_characteristics: Whitish to yellowish/tan flesh throughout the branches and base, thin and unchanging when sliced.

key_features: Tall white shaggy-scaled cylindrical cap, self-digests to black ink with age
habitat_substrate: Ground, lawns, roadsides, disturbed soil
watch_for: Tippler's Bane (Coprinopsis atramentaria, Tier B) -- eat fresh, skip alcohol for several days regardless of which inky cap it is
cap_size: 3-15 cm, oval to rounded-cylindrical (shaggy, shredded-scaly) when young, expanding to bell-shaped with age.
stem_size: 5-20 cm long x 1-2 cm thick, smooth, white, tapering toward the apex.
flesh_characteristics: White, soft flesh; the defining trait is deliquescence -- gills progress from white to pinkish to black and self-digest ("melt") into black inky liquid as the cap ages, which is why it must be eaten young/fresh.

scientific_name: Armillaria spp (A. mellea group, A. solidipes)
key_features: Honey-brown caps, white spore print, substantial ring, clustered growth
habitat_substrate: Wood, clustered on stumps/roots/buried wood
watch_for: Deadly Galerina -- see lookalike pairs table, spore print every time

citations.title: Armillaria solidipes - Honey mushroom (Beaty Biodiversity Museum, UBC)

spore_print_color: White (both A. mellea and A. solidipes).
cap_size: A. mellea: 3.5-12 cm across; A. solidipes: similar, 5-12 cm, rounded-conical when young, flattening with age.
stem_size: A. mellea: 7-20 cm long x 0.5-2 cm thick, tapering at the base, typically clustered; A. solidipes: 5-15 cm long x 0.7-1.5 cm wide, widest at the base then ending abruptly (helps distinguish it from A. mellea's tapered base).
flesh_characteristics: A. mellea flesh is whitish to very slightly pinkish and unchanging when sliced; field guides describe A. solidipes similarly as pale and non-staining.

key_features: Large to very large, smooth white skin
habitat_substrate: Ground, open areas, meadows
watch_for: Amanita button stage -- see lookalike pairs table, cut every puffball top to bottom before eating, no exceptions
spore_print_color: Not a traditional print -- spore mass (gleba) is white when young, turning olive-yellow/greenish then olive-brown to brown as it matures into powdery spore dust.
cap_size: Calvatia gigantea: 20-30+ cm across (exceptional specimens to ~50+ cm). C. booniana (western species): 15-30 cm across, occasionally over 60 cm.
stem_size: No true stem in either species. C. gigantea has a short thick cord (to ~6 cm) anchoring it to the ground; C. booniana likewise lacks a stem/stalk.
flesh_characteristics: Interior is solid white, soft/fleshy, and homogeneous (no cap-gill-stem differentiation) when young and edible -- must be checked by cutting in half to confirm pure white flesh throughout with no internal mushroom shape (rules out immature Amanita "eggs"). Turns yellow-green then olive-brown/brown powdery spore mass with age.

key_features: Small, spiny/warty white skin, interior solid white when young
habitat_substrate: Ground or wood-adjacent
watch_for: Same cut-test rule as giant puffball
spore_print_color: Olive-brown at maturity (spore mass color, not a deposited print in the gilled-mushroom sense).
cap_size: 2-7 cm wide, 3-8 cm high; pear/top-shaped fruitbody covered in small conical spines/granules that often rub off leaving a netted pattern.
stem_size: No true stem. Has a distinct sterile base (a narrower, chambered lower portion that stays spore-free) attached to thin white rhizomorphs (root-like cords).
flesh_characteristics: Interior white, firm/spongy, and homogeneous when young and edible (must be cut to confirm pure white flesh throughout); the upper spore-bearing part turns yellowish then olive-brown as it matures, while the sterile base stays yellowish-brown.

key_features: Dark gray-black trumpet shape, hollow, thin flesh
habitat_substrate: Ground, mossy hardwood/mixed areas
watch_for: Low dangerous-lookalike risk; easy to miss visually (camouflages in leaf litter) rather than misidentify
cap_size: Whole trumpet-shaped fruitbody 3-5 cm wide, 5-9 cm tall.
stem_size: No true stem and no cap/stem differentiation -- tubular becoming deeply vase/trumpet-shaped and hollow its entire length; the base simply narrows rather than forming a separate stalk.
flesh_characteristics: Thin, brittle flesh, blackish-gray to brownish-black throughout; no notable bruising, staining, or latex. Mild taste, nondescript odor fresh but can become sweet/fragrant when dried.

key_features: White, shaggy, icicle-like spine clusters, no cap/gill structure at all
habitat_substrate: Wood, living/dead hardwood or conifer (species-dependent)
watch_for: Low risk; distinctive form
cap_size: Overall mass roughly 10-20 cm broad -- a single, unbranched, rounded clump of long (often >1 cm) downward-hanging spines, distinct from the branched, multi-clustered structure of Bear's Head (H. abietis, a separate entry in this database).
stem_size: No true stem. Attaches to wood (typically hardwood wounds/dead wood) via a short, unbranched, sometimes rooting stalk-like base.
flesh_characteristics: Whitish, tough-fibrous flesh with a mild taste and odor; no notable bruising or staining.

key_features: Small orange-brown cap, exudes latex when cut, strong maple-syrup smell especially when dried
habitat_substrate: Ground, mixed/conifer duff
watch_for: Confirm the latex and smell -- other small orange Lactarius lack the maple-syrup signature
spore_print_color: Sources disagree slightly: MykoWeb reports cream-buff; MushroomExpert reports pale yellow to whitish.
cap_size: Sources disagree: MykoWeb gives 1.5-4.5 cm broad; MushroomExpert gives 2-8 cm broad (convex becoming flat or shallowly vase-shaped, dry/minutely wrinkled-bumpy, cinnamon/burnt-orange color).
stem_size: MykoWeb: 2-5 cm long x 0.4-1.0 cm thick. MushroomExpert: 2-7 cm long, up to 1.5 cm thick; stem is chalky/brittle and snaps cleanly.
flesh_characteristics: Exudes a thin, watery-white to near-colorless latex when cut -- scant, not copious or brightly colored -- that does NOT change color on air exposure (unlike many other Lactarius). Key diagnostic is a faint maple-syrup/burnt-sugar odor, weak fresh but intensifying strongly on drying.

key_features: Lilac-to-purple-brown cap and stem, pinkish-tan spore print
habitat_substrate: Ground, leaf litter, sometimes lawns/compost
watch_for: Cortinarius species can share purple-brown tones -- confirm spore print (pinkish-tan, not rusty-brown) and lack of a cobweb veil before treating as blewit

citations.title: Lepista (Clitocybe) nuda, Wood Blewit - First Nature

cap_size: Sources vary: MushroomExpert gives 3-12 cm across; First Nature gives 6-15 cm. Convex with an inrolled margin when young, becoming broadly convex to flat, purplish-lilac fading with age.
stem_size: MushroomExpert: 4-6 cm long x 2-2.5 cm thick. First Nature: 5-10 cm long x 1.5-2.5 cm thick, often with a swollen/bulbous base.
flesh_characteristics: Thick, soft, purplish-lilac to whitish flesh that does NOT change color when sliced. Fragrant, sweet/aniseed-like odor is a key diagnostic trait. Must be well cooked -- undercooked or raw specimens have caused GI upset in some people.

key_features: Gray-brown caps in dense clusters, white gills
habitat_substrate: Ground, clustered, disturbed soil
watch_for: Moderate lookalike risk within Lyophyllum/Tricholoma-adjacent genera -- confirm cluster habit and gill attachment

citations.title: Fried Chicken Mushrooms: Lyophyllum decastes - Forager | Chef

cap_size: 3-12 cm across per cap; grows in dense fused clusters of many caps, grayish-brown, often with wavy/irregular overlapping margins.
stem_size: 5-10 cm long, up to 2 cm thick; multiple stems fused together at the base within a cluster, firm/dense and "squeaky" when cut.
flesh_characteristics: White, firm flesh that does not change color or stain when cut or exposed to air. Texture is distinctively dense, tender, and squeaky/string-cheese-like rather than mealy or slimy (unlike similar-looking elm oysters).

key_features: Large rosette of gray-brown overlapping fan-shaped caps at a tree base
habitat_substrate: Wood, base of oaks (less common West Coast than eastern US)
watch_for: Low risk; distinctive form, but uncommon enough here that a positive claim deserves extra scrutiny of the base/substrate
cap_size: Whole rosette cluster 15-40 cm across, 10-30 cm high; individual overlapping fan/spoon-shaped caps 3-14 cm across, grayish-brown.
stem_size: No single true stem -- a branched system of thick, whitish, tough stalks fuses toward a common base at the tree/root, each branch terminating in one cap.
flesh_characteristics: Firm, white flesh, unchanging when sliced or exposed to air; mild pleasant odor and taste, no bruising, staining, or latex reaction.

key_features: Branched, coral-like structure, colors vary (tan, yellow, pink)
habitat_substrate: Ground, conifer forest
watch_for: Genus-level caution: some Ramaria species cause GI upset; needs species-level confirmation before eating, not a coral fungus = fine assumption
spore_print_color: Yellowish to orangish-yellow, varying by species.
cap_size: No true cap -- erect, branched/coral-shaped fruiting bodies, typically about 4-20 cm tall x 2-15 cm wide overall (varies by species).
stem_size: No true stipe; a basal stalk roughly 2-3+ cm long x to 2 cm wide, whitish and finely fuzzy, from which the coral-like branches arise.
flesh_characteristics: Brittle flesh colored white to pink/red/orange depending on species (no latex, unlike milk caps); some species such as R. formosa have bitter flesh that becomes chalk-like when dried, and several Ramaria species cause GI upset, so species-level ID matters before consumption.

scientific_name: Lactarius / Lactifluus spp (other than candy cap)
key_features: Exude latex (milk) when cut, color and taste of latex vary by species
habitat_substrate: Ground, mycorrhizal
watch_for: Large, complex genus with both good edibles and GI-upsetting species -- latex color/staining reaction and taste (bitter vs mild) separate them, needs species-level work

citations.title: LACTARIUS in the Pacific Northwest - Pacific Northwest Key Council

spore_print_color: White to pale cream/buff, sometimes yellowish; thin deposits look white while thicker deposits skew more yellow.
cap_size: Typically 2-15 cm across, though the genus overall spans roughly 0.5 cm to over 20 cm depending on species.
stem_size: Typically about 2-11 cm long x 0.3-3 cm thick.
flesh_characteristics: Cutting the flesh releases a latex ("milk") that is white or colored and may stay unchanged or shift color (e.g. turn yellow) within seconds to minutes of air exposure -- a key diagnostic trait. Use strong caution: toxic Lactarius and Russula species exist, latex should never be swallowed for identification, and any species with yellow-changing latex, lilac-staining flesh, or a strongly bitter/peppery taste should be avoided as food.

scientific_name: Suillus spp (S. lakei, S. luteus, others)
key_features: Brown-tan sticky/slimy cap, yellow pores, often a ring
habitat_substrate: Ground, conifer, often under specific pines
watch_for: Generally low dangerous-lookalike risk; peel the sticky cap skin, some people report GI sensitivity, handling can cause contact dermatitis in a minority of people
cap_size: Roughly 5-12 cm across.
stem_size: About 3-6 cm long x 1-2.5 cm thick, typically equal-width; some species (e.g. S. luteus) also bear a partial veil/ring on the stem.
flesh_characteristics: The cap cuticle is diagnostically slimy/glutinous when moist (a hallmark genus trait, often peeled off before eating); flesh is whitish to yellow, sometimes staining pinkish when sliced, and the stem base can turn bluish-green when cut in some species (e.g. S. lakei).

key_features: Rubbery, ear-shaped, brown, gelatinous
habitat_substrate: Wood, dead/dying hardwood
watch_for: Not dangerous, but has a documented mild blood-thinning effect -- worth a mention for anyone on anticoagulants, per NAMA

citations.title: Wood Ear (Tree Ear) - Missouri Department of Conservation Field Guide

cap_size: Ear/cup-shaped fruiting body about 2.5-15 cm across.
stem_size: No true stem/stipe; attaches directly to dead or decaying wood at a central or lateral point.
flesh_characteristics: Thin, gelatinous, rubbery flesh when fresh and moist, with fine hairs giving the lower surface a whitish bloom; dries hard, shrinks, and darkens to near-black, then rehydrates when wetted again.

key_features: Thin, fan-shaped, concentric colored bands, leathery/woody texture
habitat_substrate: Wood, dead hardwood/conifer
watch_for: Not a prime edible (used dried for tea/extracts); low risk, but tough and inedible fresh
cap_size: Individual caps about 2-8 cm across x 1-4 cm deep x 1-2 mm thick, usually fused into overlapping rosettes or clusters.
stem_size: No true stem; caps are bracket/fan-shaped and sessile, attaching directly to logs/stumps and often fusing with neighboring caps.
flesh_characteristics: Thin, tough, leathery (not brittle) flesh, whitish, with a distinctive very thin black line visible in cross-section separating the colorful cap surface from the flesh.

key_features: Varnished reddish-brown shelf, white growing margin when fresh
habitat_substrate: Wood, conifer base/roots
watch_for: Not a prime edible (used dried, medicinal-style); low risk, distinctive form
cap_size: Large bracket, roughly 10-50+ cm across x 5-15+ cm deep.
stem_size: Usually no true stem (sessile, laterally attached to the host tree); when a stem-like base is present it is short/stubby, lacquered, and brownish-red to reddish-brown.
flesh_characteristics: Whitish to creamy flesh, tough but not woody, lacking concentric growth-zone banding; turns black almost instantly with a KOH chemical spot test (a lab reagent test, not a natural bruise) -- no notable natural bruising on handling.

scientific_name: Agaricus campestris / A. arvensis and relatives
key_features: White to tan cap, gills pink turning chocolate-brown at maturity, white spore print
habitat_substrate: Ground, grassy areas, pastures, lawns
watch_for: Destroying Angel / Death Cap -- see lookalike pairs table, single most important Agaricus check: gills must never be white
spore_print_color: Dark brown to blackish-brown. Pink-to-chocolate-brown gill maturation, documented elsewhere in this database, remains the primary Agaricus-vs-Amanita field check.
cap_size: About 5-10 cm across, convex to broadly convex, occasionally nearly flat.
stem_size: About 3-6 cm long x 1-2 cm thick, roughly equal width, tapering slightly at the base; A. campestris has a thin, often fleeting ring, while A. arvensis tends to have a more persistent, sometimes double ring.
flesh_characteristics: White throughout, does not change color when cut or bruised in A. campestris -- a useful contrast to toxic yellow-staining lookalikes such as Agaricus xanthodermus, which discolor yellow at the cap margin/stem base and smell of phenol/iodine when cut (see The Prince entry for the full bruise-and-smell test against yellow stainer).

key_features: Almost always collected in its parasitized 'aborted' form: irregular, lumpy, brain-like or potato-like white-to-pinkish-gray masses of solid tissue, 2-10 cm across, with no true cap, gills, or stem. These are malformed Armillaria mellea (honey mushroom) fruiting bodies that have been invaded and taken over by Entoloma abortivum mycelium -- not a failed entoloma fruit body. The normal (non-aborted) form is a separate, unparasitized gilled mushroom: steel-gray convex cap 2-8 cm, gills pale gray aging to pink, farinaceous (fresh-meal/cucumber) odor, on a slender gray stem 2-8 cm. Both forms typically fruit together in the same patch, since both are triggered by the same Armillaria activity. Cut in half, the aborted form is solid and marbled white-to-pinkish throughout, not hollow or spongy.
habitat_substrate: Grows on the ground or on well-decayed wood/leaf litter in hardwood forests, always in the vicinity of Armillaria mellea (honey mushroom) activity, since the aborted form is a physical product of Entoloma parasitizing Armillaria.
season_west_coast: Late summer through fall (August-November) in the Pacific Northwest, tracking Armillaria fruiting.
range_notes: Widespread in eastern North America and also documented in the Pacific Northwest; look for it wherever honey mushrooms (Armillaria) are fruiting nearby, since the two are ecologically linked.
spore_print_color: Pink (salmon-pink), diagnostic for the normal gilled form; the aborted lumps do not produce spores and cannot be spore-printed.
cap_size: Normal form: 2-8 cm cap diameter. Aborted form: irregular masses 2-10 cm across with no defined cap.
stem_size: Normal form: 2-8 cm long, 0.5-1.5 cm thick. Aborted form: no true stem.
flesh_characteristics: Aborted form is dense, firm, and solid throughout when cut, whitish to pinkish-gray with marbled streaking, not hollow, watery, or crumbly.
watch_for: Only harvest the aborted (white lumpy) form if you can also find the normal gray-capped, pink-spored gilled form of Entoloma abortivum fruiting in the same patch nearby, confirming the parasitic pairing. Cut every lump in half: it must be solid and firm throughout (never hollow, chalky, or crumbly-dry inside), since old or rotting Armillaria clusters and other decaying fungal masses can superficially resemble aborted entoloma.

citations.title: Entoloma abortivum - Midwest American Mycological Information

key_features: Large, showy, branched coral-like fruiting body, white to creamy or pale yellowish-salmon in color, made of multiple thick branches radiating from a common base, with each branch tip hung with clusters of soft, tooth-like spines 0.5-2.5 cm long. Unlike a solid single mass, the branching structure gives it an open, many-armed look. No cap, gills, or pores -- entirely spine-bearing. Bruises and ages to yellowish or brownish tones.
habitat_substrate: Saprobic on dead or dying conifer wood, especially Douglas-fir, true fir, hemlock, and spruce logs, stumps, and standing dead trunks; causes a white rot.
season_west_coast: Fall, typically starting after the autumn rains begin (September-November), sometimes into early winter in mild years.
range_notes: Pacific Northwest specialist -- common in old-growth and mature conifer forests of coastal and Cascade-range Oregon, Washington, and north into British Columbia; less common but present in north Idaho and west Montana conifer forests.
cap_size: No cap; overall fruiting body 10-75 cm across, occasionally larger.
stem_size: No true stem; attaches directly to wood via a thick branching base.
flesh_characteristics: White, soft, spongy-fibrous flesh throughout the branches; spines are soft and brittle, breaking cleanly rather than tearing stringy.
watch_for: Distinguish from Lion's Mane (Hericium erinaceus, a separate entry in this database): Lion's Mane grows on hardwood, forms a single dense, unbranched, roughly ball- or tongue-shaped clump with all its long spines radiating from one central point, and is rare to absent in most West Coast conifer forest. If the fruiting body clearly has multiple separate branches each tipped with its own cluster of teeth, and it's growing on conifer wood, it is Bear's Head, not Lion's Mane.

key_features: Small to medium mushroom with a smooth, sticky/slimy when wet, orange-brown to dark orangish-tan cap 1-6 cm across, paling toward the margin. Gills are white to pale yellowish, attached, moderately spaced. The stem is the key feature: firm, tough, and cartilaginous, whitish and smooth near the top but developing a distinctive dark brown to blackish, fine velvety fuzz from the base upward as it ages. No ring on the stem. Grows in dense clusters fused at the base on wood.
habitat_substrate: Saprobic, growing in tight clusters on dead or dying hardwood -- stumps, logs, and buried roots (cottonwood, alder, willow, maple, box elder are common West Coast hosts).
season_west_coast: Distinctly cold-season: late fall through winter into early spring (roughly November-March), often fruiting after frost and even pushing up through light snow.
range_notes: Widespread across Oregon, Washington, California, north Idaho, and west Montana wherever suitable dead hardwood is present, especially in riparian areas with cottonwood and willow.
cap_size: 1-6 cm across.
stem_size: 2-9 cm long, 0.3-1 cm thick, tough and cartilaginous, darkening and becoming velvety-fuzzy from the base up.
flesh_characteristics: Thin, pliable, whitish flesh in the cap; stem is notably tougher and more fibrous than the cap, often trimmed away and discarded in the kitchen.
watch_for: This species fruits on wood in cold weather, the same time and substrate where the deadly Galerina marginata can also appear as small brown mushrooms. Do NOT rely on color or season to tell them apart -- take a spore print: Flammulina velutipes prints white, while Galerina marginata prints rusty brown to dull cinnamon-brown. This is the decisive, field-checkable test. Also check the stem: Galerina typically has a thin, fragile, powdery-looking stem with a delicate membranous ring partway up and lacks the dark velvety fuzz at the base; Flammulina's stem is tough/cartilaginous, ringless, and develops the visible dark velvet coating from the base upward. Never eat any small brown wood-growing mushroom without a confirmed white spore print and the velvety dark stem base present.

key_features: Small mushroom, pale tan to buff or reddish-tan (fading paler when dry, darker when wet), bell-shaped to broadly convex cap 1-5 cm with a low central bump, smooth, not sticky. Gills are white to pale tan, notably widely spaced ("distant"), and free or only narrowly attached -- not crowded and not running down the stem. The stem is thin but unmistakably tough, fibrous, and pliant/rubbery rather than brittle -- it bends and twists like a piece of string instead of snapping cleanly. Mild smell, sometimes faintly almond-like or hay-like. Commonly, but not always, arranged in arcs or rings in turf.
habitat_substrate: Saprobic in grass -- lawns, pastures, meadows, and grassy roadsides and dunes -- never on wood. Frequently forms rings or arcs of darker green, faster-growing grass with mushrooms along the ring edge, though the ring pattern can be partial or absent.
season_west_coast: Late spring through fall (May-November) on the West Coast, and nearly year-round in mild coastal California climates after rain or irrigation.
range_notes: Common and widespread throughout Oregon, Washington, and California lawns, parks, and grasslands at all elevations where turf grows; present but less frequently reported in north Idaho and west Montana.
cap_size: 1-5 cm across.
stem_size: 2-8 cm long, 1.5-6 mm thick, tough and pliant, pale, same color as cap or lighter.
flesh_characteristics: Cap flesh is thin and can dry out and revive with rehydration (marcescent), a trait fairly unusual among gilled mushrooms; stem flesh is dense, wiry, and fibrous rather than watery or brittle.
watch_for: Lawns and fairy rings can also host toxic species growing in the same ring or nearby -- notably Chlorophyllum molybdites (green-spored parasol), Clitocybe dealbata (ivory funnel, contains muscarine), and various small toxic Inocybe species. Do not identify by ring shape or lawn habitat alone. Run this combined field test: (1) bend a stem -- it must be tough and pliant, twisting like a string rather than snapping like a carrot; (2) check gill attachment and spacing -- gills should be pale cream, distinctly widely spaced, and free or barely attached, never crowded or decurrent; (3) take a spore print -- it must be white (a pink, brown, or green print rules this species out); (4) smell -- should be mild, not sweet, foul, or mealy-rancid. Treat every mushroom in the ring individually; do not assume the whole ring is one species.

key_features: Subterranean (hypogeous) fungus -- an irregularly round to potato-shaped truffle, typically marble- to golf-ball-sized, found entirely underground and never producing an above-ground mushroom. Immature specimens are whitish to beige with faint yellowish, olive, or reddish-brown tints; mature specimens develop a reddish-brown, finely fissured surface. Cut in half, the interior (gleba) is firm -- like a pencil eraser -- and white with fine marbling when young, becoming smoky brown with prominent white marbling as it matures. A ripe truffle develops a strong garlic-spice-cheese aroma 1-3 days after harvest.
habitat_substrate: Ectomycorrhizal specifically with Douglas-fir (Pseudotsuga menziesii); found in the root zone of young to early-mature Douglas-fir stands, especially plantations on former pasture or agricultural land, from sea level to about 2,000 feet elevation.
season_west_coast: October through February, the classic Oregon commercial truffle season, with harvest typically peaking December-January.
range_notes: West side of the Cascade Range and coastal mountain ranges from northern California through western Oregon and Washington into southern British Columbia; the Willamette Valley and surrounding Douglas-fir plantations are the commercial heartland.
spore_print_color: Not applicable -- truffles are hypogeous and do not release spores into the air for a print.
cap_size: Not applicable (no cap); whole truffle body typically 1.5-5 cm diameter, marble to golf-ball sized.
stem_size: Not applicable -- no stem, entirely a rounded underground body.
flesh_characteristics: Firm and solid, never spongy, hollow, or powdery when good; interior is marbled white against a brown-to-tan background at maturity, with a strong pungent aroma once ripe.
watch_for: This species cannot be reliably identified from a photograph the way an above-ground mushroom can, because it is found by smell and by raking through soil near Douglas-fir roots, not by sight. Positive identification relies on cutting the truffle open to confirm firm, solid, marbled flesh (never spongy, squishy, hollow, chalky, or powdery -- those textures indicate an unripe, rotten, or non-edible false truffle) plus the characteristic ripe aroma. If new to truffle hunting, go out with, or get confirmation from, an experienced local forager or a mycological society before eating anything dug up as a 'truffle.'

key_features: Chunky, dense chanterelle that is whitish to pale cream overall rather than golden-orange, distinguishing it from the similar and often co-occurring Pacific Golden Chanterelle. Cap 5-10 cm, broadly convex to flat, developing a central depression and becoming irregularly wavy-lobed with age, dry, whitish, bruising and aging to yellowish-orange where handled or old. False gills (blunt, forked, vein-like ridges, not true bladed gills) run down the stem, white matching the cap, also bruising yellowish-orange. Whole mushroom is notably firm, dense, and heavy for its size compared to other chanterelles.
habitat_substrate: Ectomycorrhizal with conifers, especially Douglas-fir; found on the ground, solitary to scattered, in mature and old-growth conifer forest, often partially hidden under duff or moss.
season_west_coast: Fall into early winter (September-December), overlapping with but sometimes running slightly later than golden chanterelle season.
range_notes: Pacific Northwest and northern California specialist, found in the same old-growth and mature conifer forest belt as the Pacific Golden Chanterelle, from the Cascade and Coast ranges of Washington and Oregon south into northern California.
spore_print_color: Pale yellowish to cream (very pale, similar to other Cantharellus species).
cap_size: 5-10 cm across.
stem_size: 2-5 cm long, 1-2.5 cm thick, solid, tapering toward the base.
flesh_characteristics: Thick, firm, dense white flesh throughout, solid (not hollow), sometimes yellowing slightly where cut or bruised; noticeably meatier and heavier-feeling than golden chanterelles of similar size.
watch_for: Confirm true chanterelle structure before eating: the underside should show blunt, shallow, forked, vein-like false gills that are not true bladed gills and do not separate cleanly from the cap flesh. The whitish color and forking false-gill pattern together separate this species from the golden-orange Pacific Golden Chanterelle and from true gilled lookalikes.

key_features: Large, robust Agaricus, cap 9-20+ cm (up to 30 cm in exceptional specimens), starting rounded and expanding to broadly flat with a wavy margin, covered in radiating flat brown fibrillose scales over a whitish background, giving an overall golden-brown, shaggy-scaly appearance; bruises yellowish where handled, most noticeably at the cap margin, but only mildly compared to toxic look-alikes. The single most distinctive field character is smell: a strong, sweet almond-extract or marzipan odor. Gills are free from the stem, pale at first, maturing through pink to dark chocolate-brown to nearly black. Stem is substantial, smooth and white above the ring, with fine yellowish-brown fibrous scales below, and a large, flaring, hanging, double-edged ring with yellowish patches on the underside.
habitat_substrate: Grows on the ground, saprobic/possibly weakly mycorrhizal, typically under or near conifers but also found in disturbed soil, along roadsides, gardens, and wood-chipped areas.
season_west_coast: Summer through fall (June-November), often appearing earlier in the season than many other West Coast Agaricus species.
range_notes: Widespread across Oregon, Washington, and California in conifer forest edges, landscaped areas, and disturbed ground; present in north Idaho and west Montana conifer country as well.
cap_size: 9-20 cm, occasionally to 30 cm.
stem_size: 10-20 cm long (occasionally to 35 cm), 1.5-3 cm thick, with a large flaring ring.
flesh_characteristics: Firm white flesh that bruises slowly and only mildly yellowish, most noticeable at the cap margin and near the very top of the stem; does not show a sudden, intense chrome-yellow reaction at the stem base the way the toxic yellow stainer does.
watch_for: Before eating any wild Agaricus, always run the bruise-and-smell test to rule out the yellow stainer group (Agaricus xanthodermus and relatives), which cause GI upset in most people who eat them: cut the mushroom in half lengthwise through the base of the stem and (1) look at the stem base flesh specifically -- a rapid, bright chrome-yellow stain appearing within seconds at the very base of the stem indicates a yellow stainer and the mushroom should be discarded; (2) crush or smell the cut stem base -- a phenolic, inky, or iodine-like chemical smell (often intensifying when cooked) confirms yellow stainer, whereas The Prince smells distinctly of almond extract or marzipan. Both the base-specific chrome-yellow stain AND the phenolic/ink smell should be checked together; mild, slow yellowing elsewhere on the cap or flesh is normal for The Prince and is not by itself a red flag.
